Treatment of benign malarias. Benign malarias, which are usually caused by P. vivax or, less commonly, by P. ovale or P. malariae, can be debilitating but are usually less severe than falciparum malaria. Treatment for P. vivax and P. ovale includes a radical cure: that is, cure of both the blood and liver stage infections in order to prevent re- lapse and recrudescence. Treatment of P. malariae does not include radical cure as no hypnozoites are formed dur- ing infection. Chloroquine is still generally the drug of choice (but chloroquine-resistant vivax infection has been reported from some areas—notably Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Myanmar, and Vanuatu). Chloroquine alone is adequate for P. malariae infections; for those caused by P. vivax or P. ovale a tissue schizontocide, usually pri- maquine, is added for radical cure.3,8-10 In areas where ACTs are being used as first-line treatment for P. falci- parum malaria, they may be given with primaquine for P. vivax infection as an alternative to chloroquine, with the exception of artesunate and pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine (Fansidar) as P. vivax resistance to pyrimethamine-sulf- adoxine (Fansidar) is rapidly developing.3 WHO3 recom- mends that chloroquine-resistant P. vivax may be treated with amodiaquine followed by primaquine, while the CDC10 recommends that patients not responding to chlo- roquine monotherapy or those with chloroquine-resistant infections should be given quinine sulfate plus doxycy- cline (or tetracycline) followed by primaquine; an alterna- tive is mefloquine followed by primaquine.
